tagline.text: An ethnographic museum on the UP Baguio campus devoted to Cordillera indigenous cultures

location.label: Location
location.text: UP Baguio campus, Baguio City (around Gov. Pack Road and UP Drive)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–April dry season (crowded during Panagbenga in February)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~600 (one person in Baguio: admission, local transport and a light meal; Manila round trip not included)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) in Manila, then overland to Baguio

children.text: Museo Kordilyera is the first ethnographic museum in northern Philippines, located inside the University of the Philippines Baguio (UP Baguio) campus. You can calmly explore the objects and culture of the Cordillera's indigenous peoples in a building that runs two levels underground.

Museo Kordilyera is an ethnographic museum on the University of the Philippines Baguio (UP Baguio) campus in Baguio City. It collects, preserves and exhibits objects related to the Cordillera region, its people, and their cultures and traditions, and local media describe it as the first ethnographic museum in northern Philippines. Its mission is to keep alive and enrich the cultures of the indigenous communities of the Cordillera Administrative Region, including the Bontok, Ibaloy, Ifugao, Isneg, Kalinga and Kankana-ey.

According to official UP news, the museum had a soft opening in 2016 (June 23) and was formally inaugurated about seven months later, on January 31, 2017. Representatives of Cordillera indigenous communities performed a ceremonial dance at the opening. There were three inaugural exhibits: "Batok Tattoos: Body as Archive," based on the research of director Prof. Analyn Salvador-Amores; a retrospective of the life and work of Jules de Raedt; and a photography exhibit by Roland Rabang that rethinks the ethnographic photograph.

The building has three stories, but its shape is unusual. Following the sloping terrain of the campus, only the first story sits at ground level, while the second and third are underground. Going down, you find a permanent collection area, a curatorial space for ethnographic materials, a temporary exhibition area, a visitor orientation room, an audio-visual room, a shop and a café. Some of the displayed items are reported to come from the BenCab Museum, the UP Baguio Library and Archives, the Saint Louis University Museum, and the Diocese of Baguio Museum and Archives (which item came from which source varies).

For travelers, this museum offers a quiet, cool campus setting, away from the busy downtown, where you can slowly build an understanding of Cordillera culture. If you visit it after downtown sights such as Session Road and Burnham Park, and before heading to northern highland destinations such as Sagada, Banaue and Buscalan, the background you gain makes the rest of your trip much richer. Exhibits are known to change every several months to a year, so check the museum's Facebook page for what is on before you go.

blocks.title: The first ethnographic museum in northern Philippines

children.text: The museum presents the objects and culture of the Cordillera in one place. Its themes cover the Bontok, Ibaloy, Ifugao, Isneg, Kalinga and Kankana-ey communities, making it a good source of background knowledge for highland trips.

blocks.title: A three-story building that descends underground

children.text: Only the first floor is visible above ground, while floors two and three are set into the campus slope. Because the building follows the terrain, it feels larger and cooler inside than you might expect, so you can view the exhibits calmly even on a hot day.

blocks.title: The roots of the Batok (traditional tattoo) exhibit

children.text: The first temporary exhibit, "Batok Tattoos: Body as Archive," grew out of research that looks at traditional Cordillera tattoos as records carried on the body. It is a good topic to see first if you plan to visit the tattoo village of Buscalan.

On November 15, 2019, "Handwoven Tales: The Warp and Weft of Cordillera Textiles" opened. The exhibit is based on the research of UP Baguio's Cordillera Textiles Project, and part of it can reportedly also be viewed as a 3D virtual museum on the museum's website.

Besides the permanent exhibits, there is a temporary exhibition area and a curatorial space for ethnographic materials. Exhibits are known to rotate periodically, so each visit can bring a different theme.
The lower levels are described as having a gift shop and a café. A 2025 visit blog also says the museum shop's items are worth browsing. Items and opening status vary, so check on site.

Groups can arrange a guided visit by appointment in advance. The museum's contact details include phone numbers, an email address and a Facebook page, which makes it convenient for student groups and small parties.

items.title: Half-day plan
items.subtitle: Museum visit and a campus stroll

children.text: Take a taxi or jeepney from downtown Baguio to the UP Baguio campus. The museum is known to open at
, so arriving at opening time lets you see it in peace.
Buy a ticket at the orientation room and listen to the introduction. Start on the first floor and follow the stairs and ramps down to floors two and three to see the permanent and temporary exhibits.
If the audio-visual room is open, watch a short film, then browse the museum shop for Cordillera textiles and handicraft souvenirs.
If the café is open, rest with a coffee and take a light walk around the campus.
Take a taxi or jeepney back downtown and have lunch near Session Road.
One to two hours is enough for the visit. It may take longer depending on the size of the exhibits and your interest.

items.title: Full-day plan
items.subtitle: The museum and Baguio's downtown culture route

children.text: Learn the background of Cordillera culture at Museo Kordilyera.
Head downtown and walk around Session Road and Baguio Cathedral.
After lunch, relax at Burnham Park and watch the lake and the people on bicycles.
Move to a pine-filled place such as Camp John Hay or Wright Park for a cool afternoon.
The museum is known to close at 5 p.m., so on a full-day plan it is safer to put the museum in the morning.
The museum is known to be closed on Mondays, so plan your schedule to avoid Monday.

Buses are the most common way from Manila to Baguio. Victory Liner, Dagupan Bus, Genesis and others depart almost hourly from several terminals across Metro Manila (Monumento, Cubao, Pasay and others).
The trip usually takes about
5–7 hours
. A regular air-conditioned bus costs about

one way (in 2026, roughly ₱630~650 for regular aircon depending on the departure terminal, around ₱1,000 for non-stop deluxe; fuel surcharges may push it higher). Check each company's latest announcements for current fares and schedules.
On weekends, holidays and during Panagbenga in February, tickets sell out early and roads get congested, so book in advance.
A premium bus service from the Manila airport terminals is known to exist, but check locally whether it is currently running.

items.title: From downtown Baguio to the museum

children.text: The museum is inside the UP Baguio campus (around Gov. Pack Road and UP Drive). A taxi is the easiest way; just tell the driver "UP Baguio, Museo Kordilyera."
Several jeepney routes run around the city, and jeepneys leaving the city mostly load at Burnham Park. For routes toward UP Baguio, confirm the destination at the loading area before boarding.
The taxi flag-down rate is known to be about ₱35~65 (sources differ and rates are rising) for the first
, then about ₱1.50~2 for every
. Check the meter for the exact fare; the fare from downtown to the museum depends on distance and traffic.
You can walk around inside the campus. Baguio is hilly and the weather changes often, so bring comfortable shoes and an umbrella.

Since you are viewing exhibits indoors, weather matters little, but considering the trip to the campus and your whole Baguio itinerary, the dry season is more comfortable. Baguio travel guides name November to April as the dry season with the least rainfall.
In February the Panagbenga flower festival fills the whole city, and lodging and transport become difficult. The museum itself tends to be quiet, but getting around downtown takes longer.

It is easier to stay downtown around Session Road and Burnham Park than near the museum. Downtown has many hotels, guesthouses and Airbnbs, and during Panagbenga in February or holidays, prices rise and rooms fill quickly.

For meals, have something light at the museum café if it is open, and go downtown for lunch and dinner as most visitors do. There are many local restaurants and cafés around Session Road and Baguio City Market. Opening hours and menus change often, so check locally.

If you have time after the museum, I recommend resting around the campus or at a downtown café. Baguio sits at a high elevation and is relatively cool even at midday, but walking up and down the slopes is more tiring than you might expect, so leave time after your visit to sit down and sort out what you saw. If a textile or craft caught your eye, note its name and look for the real thing in the markets and workshops of northern villages such as Sagada and Buscalan.
Before you go, check the museum's Facebook page (upbmuseokordilyera) for current exhibits and opening hours. Official announcements are updated periodically.
For group visits, contact the museum in advance to make an appointment. The museum's contact details list the phone (074) 423-0119 and an email address.
Carry cash for admission. To get a student discount, bring a valid student ID.
Because the building continues underground, visitors with limited mobility should ask in advance about mobility facilities.
Photography of exhibits may be restricted, so follow the posted notices and staff instructions.
If you visit before going to the northern highlands (Sagada, Buscalan, Banaue), it becomes easier to recognize the textiles, tattoos and crafts you saw in the exhibits.
Baguio has a large daily temperature range, so bring a light jacket. Underground galleries may feel cooler still.
The museum is known to be closed on Mondays, so check the day of the week before you go.

Before your visit, ask at the orientation room about the current exhibit layout, and staff can tell you which floor to see first. If your time is short, see the exhibit on a topic that interests you first, such as textiles or tattoos.

Opening hours and admission are based on 2017 and 2019 reports and may have changed, and some notices mention visits by appointment. Be sure to confirm by the museum's Facebook page or phone before you go.
The sources for fees and opening hours are articles several years old, so they may differ from the present.
The museum's official website is sometimes unreachable, so check the Facebook page and phone as well.
Indigenous cultural objects and tattoo exhibits carry sacred meaning for the communities. View them quietly and respect the posted notices.
Baguio has many hills and slopes, which can make walking tiring. Watch out for slippery ground on rainy days.
Make sure the taxi meter is on, and keep valuables on your person.
Baguio's main street, about
10–20 minutes
away by taxi or jeepney. Restaurants, cafés and souvenir shops cluster here.
A large park and lake in the middle of downtown. It is also where many jeepneys leaving the city load.
A pinkish church near Session Road that fits well into a downtown walking route.
A former American rest-and-recreation site with pine forest and walking trails, good for a cool afternoon after the museum.
